summary: Defines an echo function for the connectionless network layer protocol, CLNP, being standardized by ISO as an amendment to version 2 of ISO 8473.

eli5.summary: This is the ping of the CLNP world. You send a small message and wait for it to bounce back to see if the other machine is alive.

questions: how does ping work in osi
subtitle: A ping for the OSI connectionless network layer: two new packet types that let one system ask another to bounce a packet back.

tldr.problem: Gateways and links fail, and network management protocols may themselves be unreachable when they do. Operators need a simple probe inside the OSI network layer that tests whether the lowest levels of the networking software work.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines two CLNP (ISO 8473) packet types, echo-request (ERQ, type code 30) and echo-response (ERP, type code 31). The destination wraps the entire echo-request inside the data part of a new echo-response and sends it back.
tldr.outcome: Hosts and routers that support the OSI network layer MUST be able to originate an echo and respond to one. The memo replaces RFC 1139 by picking one of its two implementation alternatives.

today: RFC 1575 is a Draft Standard and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It obsoletes RFC 1139.

sections.title: Why a Network-Layer Echo
sections.content:
CLNP, the OSI connectionless network protocol defined in ISO 8473, moves data and error packets (PDUs, or simply packets) across an OSI internet. Gateways and links may fail, so operators need a way to debug and test the network layer. This memo defines an echo function for that purpose, and hosts and routers that support the OSI network layer MUST be able to both originate an echo packet and respond when one arrives.

Network management protocols can report the state of a gateway or link, but they run over protocols that may themselves lose packets, so they cannot be guaranteed to work. A simple mechanism in the network layer lets systems probe whether the lowest levels of the networking software are running correctly. The memo says it is not meant to compete with or replace network management, only to add to it.

One design rule drives everything else: the echo path through a system must be identical, or very close, to the path used by normal data. An echo path that does not succeed and fail together with the data path is not a useful diagnostic.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the tools for checking a network are broken by the same problem they are checking. So there is a tiny, simple check built into the lowest layer, like knocking on a wall to see if anyone is home.

sections.title: The Generic Echo Function
sections.content:
The memo thinks of the echo implementation as an entity that sits alongside the network layer. Its job is to accept an incoming echo-request packet, do some processing, and produce an echo-response packet. The word ping is used to mean sending an echo-request to a remote system in the expectation that an echo-response comes back.

To ping, a system builds an echo-request with normal header values and puts the target's address in as the destination NSAP address. The normal segmentation rules for a data (DT) packet apply. The packet is switched through the network like a data packet and must follow the same path as a CLNP data packet with the same header options. At the destination it goes through normal input processing and is then handed to the echo entity.

The echo entity builds a new packet, the echo-response. Its destination address is the source address of the request, and most options from the request are copied over. The entire echo-request, header and data, goes into the data part of the response, so that fields such as the request's lifetime can be examined when the response arrives. The response is relayed back like any data packet and is delivered to the entity that created the request.
sections.eli5: You write a note and mail it. The friend who gets it puts your whole note in a new envelope and mails it back, so you can see exactly what you sent and that it made the trip.

sections.title: The Two New Packet Types
sections.content:
The chosen implementation adds two packet types to ISO 8473: ERQ (echo-request) and ERP (echo-response). Apart from the type code, each is identical to a data packet in every respect.

  • The echo-request type code is decimal 30.
  • The echo-response type code is decimal 31.

Earlier drafts, including RFC 1139, offered two implementation alternatives. The authors judged that having the echo mechanisms on the Internet interoperate mattered more than backward compatibility, so this memo defines only one, consistent with one of the earlier drafts.
sections.eli5: The echo messages look just like ordinary mail, except the stamp on them says 30 for "are you there?" and 31 for "yes, here is your note back."

sections.title: Building and Answering Echo Packets
sections.content:
The echo-request function is invoked by system management to learn about the dynamic state of the network layer: whether specific network entities are reachable and what the paths between them look like. The request is built and processed by end systems and intermediate systems exactly like a data packet, with a few caveats.

  • The source and destination address fields hold Network entity titles (NETs). A NET is syntactically indistinguishable from an NSAP address, and the extra NSAP information is not needed because no data indication is ever produced from an echo-request. The destination can be an end system or an intermediate system.
  • The maximum length of the request is the maximum length of the response minus the maximum response header length, so the whole request always fits in the response's data field.
  • The request's data part may hold zero or more octets of any value. If the first octet is binary 1000 0001, an echo-response header follows, so that a router can formulate a standard echo-response.

The echo-response function runs when a request reaches the network entity named in its destination address. The response is again built like a data packet, with these rules:

  • Its source address is the request's destination address, and its destination address is the request's source address.
  • Its data part contains only the complete echo-request.
  • If the request carried an echo-response header, the responder may use it to choose header values, but the lifetime in that header must be used as the response's lifetime. Segment length and checksum are always computed by the responding entity.
  • The source routing option in the response shall not be copied from the request. If the recording of route option is copied, the second octet of the parameter value field shall be set to 3.

Whether the destination applies lifetime control before answering is a local matter, decided as it would be for a data packet. A note adds that the embedded echo-response header may be unnecessary overhead in an environment like the Internet where the request format is common.
sections.eli5: The reply is built by swapping the "to" and "from" addresses and tucking the whole original message inside. The sender can include a ready-made reply envelope, but it does not have to.

sections.title: Implementation Notes on Options
sections.content:
The memo calls its implementation notes an integral part of the specification.

  • Discarding: the ISO 8473 rules for discarding a data packet (sections 6.9 and 6.10) apply to echo packets too.
  • Error report flag: it may be set on the request, the response, or both. If a request is discarded, the error-report packet goes to the request's source address. If a response is discarded, it goes to the response's source address. The echo entity and the originator are not required to process error-report packets.
  • Lifetime: the lifetime of both packets should be the value normally used for a data packet. The memo does not define a way to vary the lifetime set in the response.
  • Priority: priority handling is a local matter and, the memo says, rarely implemented in the Internet of its day. Sending a request with a priority set may give unexpected results; if priority must be used, 0 (normal) is the safest value.
  • Source route: this option may cause packets to loop until their lifetime expires, so the memo recommends against it in both request and response. If it is used on the request, the memo does not recommend an automatically generated source route on the response.
  • Multiple requests: several processes on one machine may use the echo function. How requests and responses are matched to processes is a local matter and is not defined.
sections.eli5: There are a few house rules: use the normal time-to-live, do not give echoes special treatment, and avoid fancy routing tricks that could make a packet wander in circles.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo's security section is a single sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo. It offers no authentication or access control for echo requests, so any such protection would have to come from elsewhere.
sections.eli5: The authors did not write anything about keeping this safe from bad guys.
